transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Auriga - Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Auriga - Platform Eng), Marisol Vega (Auriga - PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial):
- Auriga is evaluating model selection for multilingual, long-context customer-facing assistant; they have strict latency targets for chat and require function/tool calling to enrich responses from internal systems.
- Key decision factors: context length (up to 65k in some use cases), multilingual quality (EN/ES/DE), cost/latency tradeoffs, and security (VPC/KMS/SOC2).
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to share pricing sheet and run dedicated benchmarks on Auriga sample data; customer to share redacted dataset and schedule security deep dive.

Topics: model selection, context length, multilingual, tool-calling, private vs dedicated hosting, benchmarking, security/compliance

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining—I'm Alex, AE at Redwood. Samira, do you want to intro?
[00:12] Samira Patel: Hey all, Samira here, solutions engineer. We'll probably do 45 to 55 minutes, talk through Auriga's use cases, latency/cost constraints, and then map model candidates and deployment modes.
[00:25] Priya Rao: Hi, thanks. I'm Priya, Head of ML at Auriga. Quick context: we run a customer-facing assistant and an internal search/chat for docs. Currently on prem K8s, vector db is Faiss-ish managed in house, retrieval pipeline is our own microservices. Key asks: long context (sometimes 60k tokens of transcript + docs), multilingual support (EN/ES/DE), and ability to call our internal tools for account lookups.
[00:52] Liam O'Connor: Platform notes — we are sensitive about data residency and keys, prefer VPC or private. We also need predictable p99 latency for chat flows (ideally < 350ms) and clear cost numbers.
[01:12] Alex Chen: Great, that's super helpful. Two big axes we'll discuss: model family and deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private). For models, given long context and multilingual, we typically look at 32k and 64k context LLMs — there are open weights like Llama-3 variants, Mistral mixtral, and also some quantized flavors. We've got Redwood-verified profiles for throughput and token-cost.
[01:36] Priya Rao: When you say Redwood-verified profiles, is that publicly available? And how often do those profiles change based on kernel selection?
[01:44] Samira Patel: We publish benchmarks in the console and docs — they show typical latency/cost on GPU types. Kernel selection is automatic in the runtime; it picks optimized kernels and quantization settings based on the model arch and the request shape. That can change effective perf a bit per model.
[02:05] Priya Rao: Our ML team cares about hallucination rates across languages. Any model recommendations for EN/ES/DE parity?
[02:13] Samira Patel: In our experience, Mistral-family and Llama-3 derivatives with instruction-tuning tend to be stronger for high-quality multilingual outputs. If you need parity, the 64k context Llama-3 variant tuned for multilingual data is a strong candidate, but it's heavier on infra. For cost-sensitive paths, a quantized 32k variant plus retrieval augmentation can be much cheaper and still meet quality targets.
[02:41] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood support function/tool calling like OpenAI-style function calls? We need structured outputs to trigger downstream services.
[02:50] Alex Chen: Yes — we support tool/function calling patterns and structured output. We also provide webhooks and a light-weight reformatting layer in the console. Note that function calling adds some latency depending on the number of round trips and whether you embed tools in the generation loop or post-process.
[03:10] Priya Rao: For our flows we prefer single-shot tool calling: model returns a JSON payload and we trigger APIs. Any constraints around size of tool descriptions or number of tools?
[03:19] Samira Patel: You can register multiple tools; the runtime will include tool schemas as needed. The practical limit is token budget — large tool schemas consume context. We recommend compact schemas and using retrieval for tool docs.
[03:33] Marisol Vega: On deployment mode: what pushes customers to Dedicated vs Private? We want both predictable latency and to keep control of keys.
[03:42] Alex Chen: Good question. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in our infra with SLA-backed latency/throughput and data isolation — you bring your workload but it's hosted. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict data residency or air-gapped needs; you run a customer-controlled control plane and we support KMS integrations. Dedicated has faster time-to-value; Private has more control and compliance overhead.
[04:05] Priya Rao: Does Private support on-prem GPUs?
[04:08] Samira Patel: Yes, we have an on-prem package. For on-prem you'll coordinate image versions and kernel builds; our team supports onboarding. There's some Ops lift but it's a fit for regulated workloads.
[04:21] Liam O'Connor: Latency — you mentioned kernel selection. If we pick a 64k context model, do we expect p50/p95 to blow up versus 32k?
[04:29] Samira Patel: Generally, cost and latency scale with context length. 64k sequences will show higher per-token latency and memory pressure; you can mitigate with KV cache strategies, prefix caching for static context, and retrieval to keep the prompt size smaller. For chat p95 targets under 350ms, many customers pick 32k or use hybrid: 64k for batch/document tasks and 32k for chat.
[04:55] Priya Rao: Are there examples of customers who do 65k plus retrieval?
[04:59] Alex Chen: Yeah, a couple verticals — legal and clinical — use long-context models with heavy retrieval and prefix caching. We have published an example case study on our docs where they shard the context and only include top-K passages into the prompt. We'll share that link after.
[05:18] Liam O'Connor: Security — SOC 2? How does Dedicated vs Hosted affect audit logs and SSO?
[05:24] Samira Patel: Hosted can be SOC 2 compliant (we provide audit logs and enterprise SSO). Dedicated also includes enhanced logging and per-customer telemetry. Private gives you full control of logs and SSO integrations. We support SAML/Okta and integrate with customer KMS for key control.
[05:42] Priya Rao: For encryption at rest in Dedicated, do we have customer-managed keys or do you manage them?
[05:48] Alex Chen: We support both. For the highest control you can use customer-managed KMS in Dedicated or Private. We'll note that in the pricing sheet options.
[05:58] Marisol Vega: For benchmarking, what do you need from us to run realistic tests?
[06:03] Samira Patel: Ideally: a redacted sample dataset that mirrors your longest contexts, a retrieval sample (top K), and the typical prompt templates. Also your latency SLO targets and expected concurrency. With that we can run a 5-10 run latency benchmark across candidate models and deployment shapes.
[06:21] Priya Rao: We can provide that. We'll need NDA considerations for sample data — do you have a secure upload?
[06:27] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll share secure upload links and an S3 presigned flow tied to the deal. Also we'll mask PII on our side during testing. We'll include that in the security doc.
[06:38] Liam O'Connor: A technical question — how does Redwood handle KV cache persistence across restarts? We want to avoid cold-start thrash.
[06:46] Samira Patel: The runtime supports persistent KV caching and warm-up policies. In Dedicated you can configure instance warm pools; for Private you control the persistence layer. Note transcription might say KV cash sometimes — it's KV cache.
[06:59] Priya Rao: Tooling: we plan to expose a small set of internal tools (account_lookup, billing_history, policy_fetch). We need type-safety on the outputs. How do you recommend we implement that?
[07:13] Samira Patel: Use strongly-typed function schemas and post-call validators. Our runtime can enforce schema validation on function outputs and reject mismatches. Also consider end-to-end tests in your CI that assert contract expectations.
[07:26] Marisol Vega: Cost — any rough numbers for 32k vs 64k on Dedicated? Ballpark to justify PoC sizing.
[07:33] Alex Chen: Ballpark is tricky without exact workload, but roughly 64k can be 2-3x token-cost compared to 32k for equivalent generated tokens because of memory and compute overhead. Dedicated commitments can reduce unit cost substantially compared to hosted on-demand; we'll include sample SKU pricing in the sheet.
[07:55] Priya Rao: Can you do adaptive serving — route heavy-context requests to cheaper variants if quality threshold met?
[08:02] Samira Patel: Yes, smart routing policy is available: you can route by latency, cost, or region. We also support fallbacks to smaller models with a quality gate — useful for keeping service available under load.
[08:16] Liam O'Connor: How about multilingual evals? We want a reproducible eval harness.
[08:21] Samira Patel: We can run automated evals on your test slices across EN/ES/DE and return BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity metrics plus human evaluation samples. We also recommend running a small human eval on critical intents.
[08:39] Priya Rao: Will you run those evals as part of the benchmark?
[08:41] Alex Chen: We can include a basic multilingual quality run; for deeper human evals we'd collaborate on the rubric and scope.
[08:48] Marisol Vega: Any red flags we should be aware of in the onboarding?
[08:51] Samira Patel: Biggest ops stuff is if you go Private/on-prem — that has more lift. Also large context models need careful batching and memory tuning; we'll help tune batching policy to meet p95 SLOs.
[09:04] Alex Chen: Ok quick recap before Qs: Redwood will send pricing sheet and Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, Samira will run benchmarks with redacted sample data, Auriga to share dataset and schedule security session.
[09:16] Priya Rao: Sounds good. A few quick Qs — how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks?
[09:21] Samira Patel: We have model version pins and rollout controls: canary, A/B, automatic fallback to older pinned versions if error rates spike. Everything is per-route and per-customer.
[09:32] Liam O'Connor: Is there a way to get telemetry into our existing Datadog stack?
[09:36] Alex Chen: Yes, we provide traces and metrics exports; Datadog + OpenTelemetry integrations are supported. We'll share the dashboard JSON for a sample route.
[09:47] Priya Rao: Any common misconfigurations you see?
[09:50] Samira Patel: Too-large prompt templates and not using retrieval — that blows up token cost. Also forgetting to compact tool schemas and over-fetching context.
[09:59] Marisol Vega: Can we see an example of a function-schema and how Redwood validates it?
[10:03] Samira Patel: We'll send an example in the follow-up email; it's a small JSON schema and the runtime enforces types.
[10:12] Priya Rao: One more on data retention — how long are logs kept in Hosted vs Dedicated?
[10:17] Alex Chen: Hosted defaults to 30 days, Dedicated can be configured up to 365 days for enterprise packages, Private you control retention. We'll include these defaults in the security doc.
[10:29] Priya Rao: Perfect.
[10:31] Alex Chen: Anything else from the Auriga side?
[10:33] Liam O'Connor: Not from me.
[10:35] Marisol Vega: No.
[10:36] Priya Rao: One ask — can you include a sample autopilot config for routing heavy-context docs to batch jobs?
[10:42] Samira Patel: Yes, we'll include a snippet of autoscaling and routing policies.
[10:46] Alex Chen: Great. We'll follow-up with the spreadsheet, secure upload link, benchmark plan, and security docs. Thanks everyone.
[10:55] Priya Rao: Thank you.
